html:
A network of rural boarding schools in Turkey, set up by law in 1940, that trained village children to go back to their villages as teachers.

Most Turks then lived in villages, and most villages had no school. The reforms of Atatürk, including the new Latin alphabet of 1928, had barely reached them. Education minister Hasan Âli Yücel and the educator İsmail Hakkı Tonguç built a plan around the idea of learning by doing.

There were 21 institutes. Pupils, boys and girls who had finished village primary school, built many of the school buildings themselves. Besides reading, maths and science they learned farming, building, crafts and music. Graduates went back as teachers and as guides for village farming and health.

The institutes produced a generation of writers who described village life from inside, among them Mahmut Makal and Fakir Baykurt. Conservatives and landowners attacked them as leftist and accused them of mixing the sexes. After the multi-party elections of 1946 they were scaled back, and in 1954 the Democrat Party government turned them into ordinary teacher schools. Many in Turkey still argue about what was lost.
sum: A network of rural boarding schools in Turkey, set up by law in 1940, that trained village children to go back to their villages as teachers.
